title: Kung Pao Chicken
subtitle: diced chicken stir-fried with dried chillies, peanuts, and Sichuan peppercorns
excerpt: Kung pao chicken is a Sichuan stir-fry of velveted chicken, dried chillies, and peanuts in a sweet-sour-savoury sauce. The whole dish comes together in under 20 minutes. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Kung pao chicken (宫保鸡丁, gōng bǎo jī dīng) is named after Ding Baozhen (1820 1886), a Qing-dynasty official and governor of Sichuan who was given the honorific Gong Bao (Palace Guardian). The dish is one of the canonical dishes of Sichuan cuisine and appears in both Sichuanese and non-Sichuanese versions across China. Fuchsia Dunlop, Land of Plenty (2001), provides the authoritative English-language account of the original Sichuan version, with its essential combination of numbing peppercorns, dried chillies, and velveted chicken.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The sauce can be mixed up to a week ahead and kept in the fridge. Velvet the chicken up to an hour ahead.

glossaryTerms.definition: A Chinese technique of marinating meat in cornflour, egg white, and rice wine before cooking. The coating protects the protein from high heat and keeps it tender and silky inside. The meat can be stir-fried directly from the marinade or briefly blanched in water or oil first.

content.text: Kung pao chicken is ready in under 20 minutes and serves four. The secret is

: marinating the chicken in cornflour, soy sauce, and Shaoxing wine before it hits the wok keeps it silky even at high heat. Mix the sauce first and have everything cut before you turn on the heat , stir-frying moves fast.
The dried chillies are for fragrance and a background heat, not to be eaten whole. The peanuts go in at the very end to keep their crunch.
Mix the chicken with the velveting cornflour, soy sauce, and Shaoxing wine. Set aside for 15 minutes. Mix the sauce ingredients together in a small bowl.

Heat {{vegetable-oil}} of oil in a wok over a high heat until smoking. Add the chicken in a single layer and let it sear for 1 minute without moving. Stir-fry for another 2 minutes until just cooked through. Remove to a plate.

In the same wok, add the dried chillies and Sichuan peppercorns and stir-fry for 30 seconds until fragrant and the chillies darken slightly. Add the garlic and ginger and stir-fry for another 30 seconds.

Return the chicken to the wok. Pour in the sauce and toss everything together over a high heat for 1 minute until the sauce thickens and coats the chicken. Add the peanuts and toss once more. Serve immediately over rice.

items.fix: The cornflour marinade is not optional . it protects the protein. Do not overcook; the chicken should reach just-cooked and will continue cooking when the sauce is added.

items.symptom: Sauce is too sweet or too sour
items.fix: Taste the sauce before adding it to the wok and adjust. Chinese black vinegar can replace some rice vinegar for more complexity.

items.cause: Seeds left in or too many chillies
items.fix: Shake seeds out before cooking. The chillies are flavouring agents . you are not meant to eat them whole.

content.text: Kung pao chicken is cooked across China and familiar globally, though the overseas version is often sweeter and less numbing than the Sichuan original. The Sichuan version relies on the tingling of Sichuan peppercorn (the má in the region's má là, or numbing-spicy, flavour profile) alongside the heat of the dried chillies (là). Both are important and neither should be omitted.
